mark_split.label: Why the second child is at risk

steps.label: What it is
steps.why: The trouble arises only when the foetus carries an antigen the mother does not have, so the combination of parents matters.
common_mistakes: Reversing the parents. The mother is Rh negative and the foetus Rh positive.
Calling it an infection. It is an alloimmune condition.
steps.memory_tip: Rh negative mother, Rh positive baby.
steps.margin_note: Name the two blood types in the first line.
lines: Erythroblastosis foetalis, or haemolytic
disease, is an alloimmune condition that
develops in an Rh positive foetus whose
father is Rh positive and whose mother is
Rh negative.
The genetic consequence is Rh
incompatibility between the mother (Rh⁻)
and the growing foetus (Rh⁺).

steps.label: How the mother is sensitised
steps.why: The two blood supplies are normally kept apart, so the mother only meets the foetal antigen when the placenta tears at birth.
common_mistakes: Saying the bloods mix throughout pregnancy. They are kept separate.
steps.memory_tip: The bloods meet at delivery, not before.
steps.margin_note: Say exactly when the two bloods meet.
lines: At the time of delivery, the Rh⁺ blood
cells may enter the mother's blood through
the ruptured placenta.
The mother's immune system is sensitised
and anti-Rh antibodies are produced.

steps.label: Why the second child is at risk
steps.why: By the second pregnancy the antibodies already exist, and unlike red cells they can cross the placenta.
common_mistakes: Saying the first child is affected. The first child is safe.
Leaving out that the antibodies cross the placenta.
steps.memory_tip: First child safe, second child at risk.
steps.margin_note: Explain why the first child escapes.
lines: The first child is safe, because the
delivery is over before the antibodies
form.
During a second pregnancy, if the child is
Rh positive, these antibodies cross the
placenta and enter the foetal blood.
The blood cells of the Rh positive foetus
are destroyed, causing haemolytic disease
of the new born.

steps.label: The name and prevention
steps.why: The foetus replaces the destroyed cells with immature ones called erythroblasts, and those give the disease its name.
common_mistakes: Leaving out why the disease is called erythroblastosis.
Naming the wrong injection. It is anti-D.
steps.memory_tip: Erythroblasts in the blood give the disease its name; anti-D prevents it.
steps.margin_note: End with the prevention. The name and the prevention share this mark, so give both.
lines: To make up the loss, the foetal
haemopoietic system releases erythroblasts,
an early stage of red blood cells, into the
circulation. That is why the disease is
called erythroblastosis foetalis.
The mother is given anti-D, that is anti-Rh
antibodies, right after the delivery of the
first Rh positive child.

lines.text: This stops her immune system being sensitised

insider_note: The whole answer turns on why the FIRST child is safe. Say that antibody formation takes time and the first delivery is already over.
